content: It is crucial to identify and reach key populations and individuals with limited access to clinical and community-based services. These groups may include sex workers, people who inject drugs, men who have sex with men, transgender individuals, adolescent girls, migrants, mobile populations, older women, and certain high-risk occupational groups. As antiretroviral therapy (ART) coverage expands and programs mature, increasing access to second-line regimens becomes a programmatic priority. Scaling up viral load monitoring is essential to accurately identify treatment failure and avoid unnecessary switching to second-line regimens. Viral load monitoring also plays a central role in areas where ART is being widely expanded to reduce HIV incidence. As individuals initiate treatment earlier and remain on it longer, monitoring the quality of service delivery and strengthening service linkages to improve retention throughout the care cascade is critical to optimizing treatment outcomes and long-term program performance. Estimating the costs associated with implementing new recommendations is a key step in the rollout process. Various costing tools and resources are available to assist countries in estimating the costs and budgeting for HIV-related interventions and services. The Spectrum suite of models and analytical tools supports decision-making and includes applications such as the AIDS Impact Model (AIM) and Goals (Cost and Impact of HIV Interventions). These tools can estimate the impact of new recommendations on ART-related deaths averted, infant infections prevented through PMTCT (prevention of mother-to-child transmission), and the costs and needs for adult, pediatric, and PMTCT treatments. Key data required for these estimates include demographic projections, HIV incidence trends, historical ART coverage data, PMTCT intervention data, and unit costs for ART and PMTCT. The Goals module can estimate the number of adult HIV infections averted by ART under different eligibility criteria and scale-up rates. Inputs required include the distribution of the adult population by risk group (e.g., serodiscordant couples, individuals with casual partners, sex workers, men who have sex with men, transgender individuals, and people who inject drugs), sexual behavior data, and needle-sharing practices. OneHealth is another software tool designed to strengthen health system analysis, costing, and financing scenarios at the country level. It is tailored for lowand middle-income countries and provides a unified framework for planning, costing, impact analysis, budgeting, and financing strategies for major diseases and health system components. WHO and collaborating organizations have also developed tools to assist with drug quantification and supply management. Monitoring and evaluation frameworks must be adapted to track the implementation and impact of new guidelines on HIV programs and individuals receiving ART. This includes assessing the effectiveness of interventions and service linkages along the treatment and care cascade. Monitoring individualand population-level outcomes, such as toxicity, adverse events, drug resistance, viral suppression, mortality, survival, and incidence, is essential to evaluate program impact. Data collection methods include routine facility reporting, population-based surveys, cohort observations, and periodic evaluations. Efforts should also focus on integrating monitoring systems for PMTCT, TB, and ART services and incorporating HIV drug resistance monitoring into routine health information systems. Civil society involvement in monitoring and evaluation activities is critical to understanding successes and failures, particularly in assessing the experiences and perceptions of people living with HIV and key populations. WHO is developing a consolidated guide on monitoring and evaluating HIV in the health sector, aligning existing approaches with new recommendations and emerging areas for HIV monitoring and evaluation. Programs are increasingly focusing on critical outcomes, such as viral load suppression and immune reconstitution, as well as broader impacts like HIV-related mortality and incidence. However, unintended outcomes, such as drug resistance and ARV-related toxicities, must also be measured. Surveillance of HIV drug resistance is a vital component of national HIV programs. Drug resistance can lead to virological failure, increased reliance on second-line regimens, and reduced effectiveness of ARV-based prevention strategies. WHO has developed standardized assessment strategies for monitoring early warning indicators, acquired drug resistance, pre-treatment resistance, and transmitted resistance. These efforts aim to optimize ART regimens and inform policy decisions.
